health.cpu_sensor.title: Enable accurate CPU temperature
health.cpu_sensor.estimated: Showing an estimated {0} from the Windows ACPI thermal zone (nothing to install). Click the button and PC Check will install the signed PawnIO driver and read the real sensors inside the CPU.
health.cpu_sensor.none: This PC exposes no ACPI thermal zone, so there is no CPU temperature yet. Click the button and PC Check will download, verify and install the PawnIO driver – once, no app restart needed.

health.no_device_sensors: This device has no live sensors.

compat.unknown: Could not be determined (administrator rights needed).
compat.ram_capacity.title: RAM capacity
compat.ram_capacity.rec: Upgrade to at least 8 GB (16 GB recommended) for smooth Windows 11 and web browsing.
compat.ram_channel.title: Dual channel
compat.ram_channel.single: Only 1 RAM stick in {0} slots → running in single channel, which halves memory bandwidth.
compat.ram_channel.dual: {0} RAM sticks in {1} slots – dual channel capable.
compat.ram_channel.rec: Add a matching stick (same capacity/speed) to run dual channel for a noticeable speed-up, especially with integrated graphics.
compat.ram_matched.title: Matched RAM sticks
compat.ram_matched.mismatch: RAM sticks differ in capacity or speed: {0}.
compat.ram_matched.different_brand: Same capacity and speed but different brand/part – usually fine; if the PC freezes or blue-screens, test one stick at a time.
compat.ram_matched.ok: All sticks share the same capacity, speed and part number.
compat.ram_matched.rec: Mismatched RAM runs at the slowest stick's speed and may lose dual channel or cause errors. Use identical sticks.
compat.ram_speed.title: RAM speed
compat.ram_speed.slow: RAM is running at {0} MHz, below its rated {1} MHz.
compat.ram_speed.ok: RAM is running at its rated {0} MHz.
compat.ram_speed.rec: Enable XMP (Intel) / EXPO, DOCP (AMD) in the BIOS so RAM runs at its rated speed. Mixed sticks run at the slowest one's speed.
compat.ram_speed.rec_laptop: Laptops are usually limited by the CPU/motherboard – this is normal.
compat.ram_upgrade.title: RAM upgrade options
compat.ram_upgrade.detail: Motherboard supports up to {0} in {1} slots ({2} free). RAM type: {3}.
compat.win11_cpu.title: Windows 11 supported CPU
compat.win11_cpu.pass: {0} is on the supported list (or the PC already runs Windows 11).
compat.win11_cpu.fail: {0} is not on the Windows 11 supported CPU list (needs Intel Core 8th gen+ or AMD Ryzen 2000+).
compat.win11_cpu.unknown: Could not tell for sure whether {0} is supported. Check with Microsoft's PC Health Check app.
compat.tpm.title: TPM 2.0
compat.tpm.none: No TPM found (it may be disabled in the BIOS).
compat.tpm.rec: Enable TPM / Intel PTT / AMD fTPM in the BIOS. Most PCs from 2017 onwards have one.
compat.uefi.title: UEFI boot
compat.uefi.yes: The PC boots in UEFI mode.
compat.uefi.legacy: The PC boots in Legacy BIOS (CSM) mode.
compat.uefi.rec: Convert the system drive to GPT (mbr2gpt) and switch the BIOS to UEFI. Back up your data first.
compat.secureboot.title: Secure Boot
compat.secureboot.rec: Turn on Secure Boot in the BIOS (requires UEFI mode) for better security and Windows 11 compliance.
compat.win11_storage.title: System drive size
compat.win11_storage.detail: System drive is {0} (Windows 11 needs at least 64 GB).
compat.win11_summary.title: Ready for Windows 11?
compat.win11_summary.ready: This PC meets the main Windows 11 requirements.
compat.win11_summary.blocked: This PC does not meet some Windows 11 requirements (see the failed items above).
compat.win11_summary.maybe: Could not fully determine. Run as administrator or use Microsoft's PC Health Check.
compat.os_arch.title: 64-bit Windows
compat.os_arch.32bit: Running 32-bit Windows – RAM is limited and many new apps are unsupported.
compat.os_arch.ram_wasted: 32-bit Windows can only use about 3.5 GB of the {0} installed!
compat.os_arch.rec: The CPU supports 64-bit: reinstall 64-bit Windows to use all RAM and run modern software.
compat.system_ssd.title: Windows on an SSD
compat.system_ssd.hdd: Windows runs on a hard disk ({0}) – booting and opening apps will be slow.
compat.system_ssd.rec: Upgrading to an SSD (SATA or NVMe) is the most effective speed-up, 5–10× faster than a hard disk.
compat.system_usb.title: System drive over USB
compat.system_usb.detail: Windows is running from a USB drive – speed and stability are limited.
compat.virtualization.title: CPU virtualization (VT-x / AMD-V)
compat.virtualization.on: Virtualization is enabled – Android emulators, WSL and VMs will work.
compat.virtualization.off: Virtualization is disabled in the BIOS.
compat.virtualization.rec: Enable Intel VT-x / AMD SVM in the BIOS if you use Android emulators (BlueStacks, LDPlayer, NoxPlayer), WSL, Hyper-V or virtual machines.
compat.multi_av.title: Antivirus conflict
compat.multi_av.rec: Keep only one antivirus. Running several at once slows the PC down and causes conflicts.
compat.bios.title: BIOS version
compat.bios.rec: The BIOS is fairly old. Check the vendor's support page for updates (better RAM/CPU compatibility, security). Only update on AC power and never interrupt it.
compat.gpu_driver.title: Graphics driver
compat.gpu_driver.basic: Using Microsoft Basic Display driver – the graphics driver is not installed.
compat.refresh.title: Refresh rate: {0}
compat.refresh.low: Display is running at {0} Hz but supports up to {1} Hz.
compat.refresh.ok: Running at {0} Hz (the highest at the current resolution).
compat.refresh.rec: Open Advanced display settings and pick the highest refresh rate for smoother motion (especially for gaming). Use a suitable DisplayPort/HDMI cable.
compat.resolution.title: Resolution: {0}
compat.resolution.low: Using {0}×{1}, the display supports up to {2}×{3}. Use the native resolution for sharp text (adjust Scale if text is too small).
drivers.all_ok: All devices have drivers and are working properly.
drivers.search: Search by device name, class, provider...
drivers.outdated_detail: Driver dated {0} – fairly old, check for a newer version.
drivers.unsigned_detail: Driver is not digitally signed – it may be unsafe or unstable.
drivers.generic_detail: Using a generic Windows driver instead of the vendor driver.

junk.user_temp.desc: %TEMP% folder – temporary files created by apps (only files older than 24 hours).
junk.windows_temp.name: Windows temporary files
junk.windows_temp.desc: C:\Windows\Temp – temporary files of the system and installers.
junk.wu_cache.name: Windows Update cache
junk.wu_cache.desc: Updates that were downloaded and installed (SoftwareDistribution\Download).
junk.delivery_opt.name: Delivery Optimization
junk.delivery_opt.desc: Cache used to share updates between PCs.
junk.error_reports.name: Windows error reports
junk.error_reports.desc: Error reports (WER) sent or queued for Microsoft.
junk.windows_logs.name: Old Windows logs
junk.windows_logs.desc: Log, etl and cab files older than 7 days in C:\Windows\Logs.
junk.thumbnails.name: Thumbnail cache
junk.thumbnails.desc: File Explorer thumbnails, rebuilt automatically (Explorer may lock them).
junk.crash_dumps.name: Crash dumps
junk.crash_dumps.desc: Minidump, MEMORY.DMP – keep them if you are investigating blue screens.
junk.shader_cache.name: Shader cache (DirectX/GPU)
junk.shader_cache.desc: Rebuilt automatically; games may stutter slightly on the next launch.
junk.browser.name: {0} cache
junk.browser.desc: Web page cache only – passwords, history and cookies are kept. Close the browser to clean more.
junk.recycle.name: Recycle Bin
junk.recycle.desc: Deleted files in the Recycle Bin – check first, they cannot be restored afterwards.
junk.cleaned_skipped: Freed {0}. Skipped {1} files that are in use.
junk.confirm:

junk.disk_cleanup_hint: Want to safely remove old Windows updates, the Windows.old folder or old installers? Use Windows' Disk Cleanup.

startup.hint: Disabling startup programs makes Windows boot faster. Disabling is not uninstalling – you can still open the app normally.
startup.failed: Could not change the startup state of {0}.
issues.none: No issues found. Your PC is in good shape!
issues.events_title: System errors in the last {0} days
issues.events_desc: Collected from the Windows Event Log: blue screens, unexpected shutdowns, hardware errors, disk errors, app crashes.
issues.tools_desc: Built-in Windows tools, one click away. Heavy commands open in their own window so you can follow progress.
events.power_loss_hint: Power loss, hard freeze or holding the power button.
events.whea_hint: Errors from CPU, RAM, PCIe or overclocking.
events.disk_hint: Bad sectors, I/O errors, controller resets or NTFS errors.
events.tdr_hint: The screen goes black and recovers (TDR).

fix.result.unsupported: This action is not supported yet.
fix.result.restarting: The PC will restart in 10 seconds.
fix.result.restore_point_fail: Could not create a restore point. Turn on System Protection for drive C: in the window that opened (or one was already created in the last 24 hours).
fix.result.restart_needed: Network reset done. Restart the PC to finish.
fix.result.no_battery: Could not create a battery report (no battery?).
fix.result.uninstaller_started: Opened the uninstaller for {0}. Press "Refresh" when it is done.
tool.sfc-dism.name: Repair system files
tool.sfc-dism.desc: DISM + SFC: scan and repair corrupted Windows files (10–30 min).
tool.sfc-dism.confirm: Open a command window that runs DISM /RestoreHealth and then SFC /scannow to repair corrupted system files. It takes 10–30 minutes; do not turn off the PC meanwhile. Continue?
tool.cpu-sensor.confirm: PC Check will download the official PawnIO driver (free, open source, digitally signed) from GitHub, verify its signature and install it silently – no app restart needed. The driver lets the app read the CPU's internal temperature sensors (like HWiNFO or Core Temp do). Continue?
tool.chkdsk.name: Check disk (CHKDSK)
tool.chkdsk.desc: Scan the NTFS file system for errors without a restart.
tool.chkdsk.confirm: Run CHKDSK /scan to check the file system. It may take a few minutes. Continue?
tool.mdsched.name: Test RAM
tool.mdsched.desc: Windows Memory Diagnostic – tests RAM on the next restart.
tool.mdsched.confirm: Windows Memory Diagnostic will open so you can restart now or test on the next boot. Save your work first. Continue?
tool.restore-point.name: Create restore point
tool.restore-point.desc: Create a System Restore point before changing the system.
tool.restore-point.confirm: Create a System Restore point? Windows allows one every 24 hours.
tool.flushdns.name: Flush DNS cache
tool.flushdns.desc: Fixes some websites failing to load.
tool.network-reset.name: Reset network
tool.network-reset.desc: Reset Winsock and TCP/IP when the connection is broken.
tool.network-reset.confirm: Reset Winsock and TCP/IP. A restart is needed afterwards; static IP/VPN settings may need to be set up again. Continue?
tool.wu-reset.name: Fix Windows Update
tool.wu-reset.desc: Refresh the update cache when Windows Update is stuck or failing.
tool.wu-reset.confirm: Stop Windows Update services, rename SoftwareDistribution and catroot2, then restart the services. The visible update history may be emptied. Continue?
tool.scan-devices.name: Scan for hardware changes
tool.scan-devices.desc: Detect new devices and install available drivers.
tool.wsreset.name: Repair Microsoft Store
tool.wsreset.desc: Clear the Microsoft Store cache when the Store misbehaves.
tool.battery-report.name: Battery report
tool.battery-report.desc: Detailed battery capacity and usage history (laptops).
tool.cleanmgr.name: Disk Cleanup
tool.cleanmgr.desc: Remove old updates and Windows.old with Windows' own cleaner.
tool.reliability.name: Reliability history
tool.reliability.desc: Reliability Monitor – errors and crashes by day.
tool.eventvwr.name: Event Viewer
tool.devmgmt.name: Device Manager
tool.powercfg.name: Power options
tool.uac.name: UAC settings
tool.uac.desc: Turn User Account Control back on.
tool.performance.name: Performance options
tool.performance.desc: Visual effects and virtual memory (page file).
bugcheck.hint.ram: This error is usually caused by RAM: run "Test RAM", reseat or test one stick at a time, disable XMP/overclocking.
bugcheck.hint.driver: This error is usually caused by a driver: update drivers (graphics, network, chipset), remove recently installed software/drivers, run "Repair system files".
bugcheck.hint.gpu: Graphics-related error: reinstall the latest GPU driver, check GPU temperature, remove GPU overclocks.
bugcheck.hint.disk: Storage-related error: back up your data now, run CHKDSK, check S.M.A.R.T health and the drive cable/slot.
bugcheck.hint.hardware: Hardware error (CPU/RAM/PSU/motherboard): remove overclocks, check temperatures and the power supply, update the BIOS.
bugcheck.hint.system: Possibly corrupted system files or conflicting software: run "Repair system files", update Windows and drivers.
issue.cpu_hot.title: CPU is overheating ({0}°C)
issue.cpu_hot.detail: CPU temperature is {0}°C (load {1}%). Sustained heat makes the CPU throttle (slow down), freeze or shut down.
issue.cpu_hot.detail_estimated: The estimated temperature (ACPI thermal zone) is {0}°C at {1}% CPU load. Enable accurate CPU temperature to see the real value.
issue.cpu_hot.rec: Clean dust from fans and vents, replace thermal paste (if older than 2 years), make sure fans spin. On laptops, raise the back or use a cooling pad.
issue.cpu_idle_hot.title: CPU unusually hot at idle ({0}°C)
issue.cpu_idle_hot.detail: CPU is at {0}°C with only {1}% load. A healthy idle CPU is typically 35–55°C.
issue.pawnio.title: CPU temperature not available
issue.pawnio.detail: Windows does not report a CPU temperature on this PC. PC Check can install the PawnIO driver (free, open source, signed) to read the sensors inside the CPU.
issue.pawnio.rec: Click "Enable accurate CPU temperature" – PC Check downloads, verifies and installs it, no app restart needed.
issue.pawnio.title_estimated: CPU temperature is only an estimate
issue.pawnio.detail_estimated: Showing about {0}°C from the Windows ACPI thermal zone (nothing to install) – this is often lower or slower than the real CPU temperature.
cpu_sensor.stage.download: Downloading the PawnIO driver from GitHub…
cpu_sensor.result.ok: PawnIO driver installed. CPU temperature will appear in a moment.
cpu_sensor.result.reboot: PawnIO driver installed. Restart the PC to start reading CPU temperature.
cpu_sensor.result.failed: Driver installation failed (code {0}). Try again or install it manually from pawnio.eu.
cpu_sensor.result.download_failed: Could not download the driver. Check your Internet connection and try again.
cpu_sensor.result.untrusted: The downloaded file has no valid digital signature, so it was discarded for safety.
cpu_sensor.result.cancelled: Cancelled – administrator permission is required to install the driver.
issue.gpu_hot.title: Graphics card is overheating ({0}°C)
issue.gpu_hot.detail: GPU is at {0}°C. Excessive heat can cause stutter, freezes or driver crashes.
issue.gpu_hot.rec: Clean the graphics card fans, improve case airflow, consider capping FPS or undervolting.
issue.battery_wear.title: Battery worn {0}%
issue.battery_wear.detail: Design capacity {0:N0} mWh, now only {1:N0} mWh when fully charged. Cycle count: {2}.
issue.battery_wear.rec_replace: The battery is heavily worn and runtime is noticeably shorter. Consider a genuine replacement.
issue.battery_wear.rec_care: Avoid draining to zero or staying at 100% all the time; enable the vendor's 80% charge limit if available.
issue.ram_usage.title: RAM almost full ({0}%)
issue.ram_usage.detail: {0} of {1} in use. When RAM is full Windows swaps to disk, which makes the PC slow and choppy.
issue.ram_usage.rec: Close unused browser tabs and apps, disable startup programs, or add more RAM.
issue.gpu_error.title: Graphics card reports an error: {0}
issue.gpu_error.rec: Reinstall the latest graphics driver from the vendor. If it persists, check that the card is seated firmly and has its power cables connected.
issue.disk_failing.title: Drive is failing: {0}
issue.disk_failing.detail: Drive {0} reports bad health (S.M.A.R.T). Data may be lost at any time.
issue.disk_failing.rec: BACK UP YOUR DATA NOW to another drive or the cloud, then replace the drive.
issue.disk_warning.title: Drive warning: {0}
issue.disk_warning.detail: Drive {0} reports a warning state. Errors may be starting to appear.
issue.ssd_wear.title: SSD {0} has used {1}% of its life
issue.ssd_wear.detail: The SSD has used {0}% of its rated endurance, about {1}% remains.
issue.ssd_wear.rec: Back up regularly and plan to replace the SSD when less than 10% life remains.
issue.disk_errors.title: Drive has read/write errors: {0}
issue.disk_errors.rec: Run CHKDSK and back up important data. If errors keep increasing, replace the drive.
issue.disk_hot.title: Drive {0} is hot ({1}°C)
issue.disk_hot.detail: Drive temperature is {0}°C, above the recommended {1}°C. Heat reduces speed and lifespan.
issue.disk_hot.rec: Improve case airflow, add a heatsink to NVMe SSDs, keep drives away from heat sources.
issue.low_space.title: Drive {0} is almost full ({1} free)
issue.low_space.rec_system: The system drive needs at least 15–20% free space for updates and smooth operation. Clean junk, uninstall unused apps, move data to another drive.
issue.low_space.rec_data: Remove some data or move it to another drive.
issue.driver_missing.title: Driver not installed: {0}
issue.driver_error.title: Device error: {0}
issue.driver_missing.rec: Install the driver from Windows Update (optional drivers) or the PC/motherboard vendor's support page. You can search by hardware ID.
issue.driver_error.rec: Uninstall the device in Device Manager, scan for hardware changes and install the latest driver. If it still fails, the hardware may be faulty.
issue.driver_basic_display.title: Graphics driver not installed
issue.driver_basic_display.detail: Windows is using "Microsoft Basic Display Adapter" – no hardware acceleration, no resolution/refresh-rate control, poor gaming and video playback.
issue.driver_basic_display.rec: Download the graphics driver from NVIDIA / AMD / Intel or your laptop vendor.
issue.driver_generic_audio.title: Using the generic audio driver
issue.driver_generic_audio.detail: The sound card uses Microsoft's generic "High Definition Audio" driver – some features (mic, jack detection, audio effects) may be missing.
issue.driver_generic_audio.rec: Install the audio driver (Realtek...) from the PC/motherboard vendor's support page.
issue.driver_unsigned.title: {0} unsigned drivers
issue.driver_unsigned.rec: Unsigned drivers may be unsafe. Replace them with official versions from the vendor.
issue.driver_outdated.title: {0} outdated drivers
issue.driver_outdated.detail: Drivers not updated for a long time: {0}.
issue.driver_outdated.rec: Updating drivers fixes bugs and improves performance and security. Prioritize graphics, network and audio.
issue.driver_disabled.title: {0} devices are disabled
issue.driver_disabled.rec: If you did not disable them on purpose, re-enable them in Device Manager.
issue.bsod.title: {0} blue screens in {1} days
issue.bsod.detail_dump: Minidump files found (latest {0:g}) – the PC has had blue screen crashes.
issue.power_loss.title: {0} unexpected shutdowns in {1} days
issue.power_loss.detail: Windows recorded improper shutdowns (power loss, hard freeze or holding the power button).
issue.power_loss.rec_laptop: Check the battery/charger and CPU temperature. If it shuts down when hot, clean the cooling system.
issue.power_loss.rec_desktop: Check that the power supply (PSU) is adequate and stable, the power cable/outlet and CPU/GPU temperatures. Consider a UPS if power is unstable.
issue.whea_fatal.title: Fatal hardware errors ({0}×)
issue.whea.title: Many corrected hardware errors ({0}×)
issue.whea.detail: {0} fatal and {1} corrected errors in {2} days (WHEA – from CPU, RAM or PCIe slots).
issue.whea.rec: Remove CPU/RAM overclocks, test RAM, update the BIOS and chipset drivers. Reseat PCIe/NVMe cards.
issue.disk_events.title: Disk reported errors {0} times in {1} days
issue.disk_events.detail: Windows recorded read/write errors or bad sectors on a drive ({0}).
issue.disk_events.rec: Back up your data now, run CHKDSK and check drive health. Repeated errors usually mean the drive is failing.
issue.storage_reset.title: Drive was reset {0} times in {1} days
issue.storage_reset.detail: The storage controller had to reset the device – this usually freezes the PC for a few seconds.
issue.storage_reset.rec: Check the SATA cable/M.2 slot, update SSD firmware and chipset/storage drivers.
issue.ntfs.title: File system corruption ({0}×)
issue.ntfs.detail: Windows detected a corrupted NTFS file system structure.
issue.ntfs.rec: Run CHKDSK to repair the file system.
issue.tdr.title: Graphics driver hung {0} times in {1} days
issue.tdr.detail: The display driver stopped responding and had to restart (screen flashes black).
issue.tdr.rec: Reinstall the latest graphics driver, check GPU temperature, remove GPU overclocks.
issue.low_memory.title: System ran low on memory ({0}×)
issue.low_memory.detail: Windows warned that virtual memory was exhausted – apps may close unexpectedly.
issue.low_memory.rec: Re-enable the page file (system managed), close apps or add more RAM.
issue.app_crash.title: {0} apps crash frequently
issue.app_crash.detail: Apps that crashed/hung repeatedly in {1} days: {0}.
issue.app_crash.rec: Update or reinstall these apps. If many apps crash, run "Repair system files" and test RAM.
issue.not_admin.title: Not running as administrator
issue.not_admin.detail: Some checks (CPU temperature, TPM, S.M.A.R.T, Prefetch, system folder cleanup) need administrator rights.
issue.win10_eos.title: Windows 10 is out of support
issue.win10_eos.detail: Microsoft stopped security updates for Windows 10 on {0:d}. The PC is exposed to malware and unpatched vulnerabilities.
issue.win10_eos.rec: Upgrade to Windows 11 if the PC qualifies (see the Compatibility page).
issue.win_version_eos.title: Windows {0} is out of support
issue.win_version_eos.detail: Version {0} stopped receiving security updates on {1:d}. The latest version is {2}.
issue.win_version_eos.rec: Use Windows Update to move to the latest version (free).
issue.pending_reboot.title: Restart required
issue.pending_reboot.detail: Updates or system changes are waiting for a restart to finish.
issue.uptime.title: PC not restarted for {0} days
issue.uptime.detail: Restarting regularly frees memory and applies updates.
issue.uptime.detail_fast: Fast Startup is on, so "Shut down" does not refresh the system – use "Restart" regularly.
issue.no_av.title: No active antivirus
issue.no_av.detail: The PC has no real-time protection against malware.
issue.no_av.rec: Turn Microsoft Defender back on in Windows Security (free and good enough for most users).
issue.av_outdated.title: Antivirus definitions are out of date
issue.firewall.title: Firewall is off
issue.firewall.detail: Windows Firewall is off for network profiles: {0}.
issue.uac.title: UAC is disabled
issue.uac.detail: User Account Control is off – malware can run with admin rights without asking.
issue.activation.title: Windows is not activated
issue.activation.detail: Windows is not activated – some personalization features are restricted.
issue.updates.title: Windows not updated for {0} days
issue.updates.detail: The latest update was installed on {0:d}. Regular updates patch security vulnerabilities.
issue.pagefile.title: Page file is disabled
issue.pagefile.detail: With {0} of RAM, disabling the page file easily leads to out-of-memory errors and crashes.
issue.windows_old.title: Previous Windows installation found (Windows.old)
issue.windows_old.detail: Windows.old usually takes 10–30 GB. If you do not need to roll back, remove it with Disk Cleanup / Storage Sense.
issue.junk.title: {0} of junk files can be cleaned
issue.junk.rec: Cleaning junk files frees up disk space.
issue.bloat.title: {0} junk / unwanted programs
issue.bloat.rec: Remove adware, fake "optimizers" and toolbars to make the PC lighter and safer.
issue.bloat.rec_crack: A crack tool was found – these often carry malware. Remove it now and run a full antivirus scan.
issue.unused.title: {0} programs unused for over {1} days
issue.unused.rec: Uninstall software you no longer use to free space and reduce background processes.
issue.startup.title: {0} programs start with Windows
issue.startup.detail: Too many programs launching at boot slow down startup and use RAM.
issue.startup.rec: Disable the ones you do not need (chat apps, updaters, game launchers...).
report.title: PC check report
report.footer: Generated by PC Check · scan took {0:0.0} s
settings.language_desc: Display language of the app and reports.
settings.autoscan_desc: Run a full scan as soon as PC Check opens.
settings.live_desc: Refresh temperatures and CPU/RAM load every 2 seconds (paused while minimized).
settings.report_desc: Export the scan results to an HTML file to keep, print or send to a technician.
settings.admin_no: No administrator rights – some checks are limited.
settings.shortcuts: Shortcuts: F5 – rescan · Ctrl+S – export report · Esc – close dialog.
settings.credits: Sensors read with LibreHardwareMonitor (MPL-2.0). System information via WMI and Windows APIs.
page.widget.title: Desktop widget
page.widget.subtitle: A small floating panel showing temperatures, CPU, RAM, GPU, network and disk in real time. Drag it anywhere on the screen.
widget.visible_desc: The widget keeps running when you close the PC Check window. Double-click the widget to reopen the app.
widget.topmost_desc: Keep the widget above all other windows.
widget.locked_desc: Prevent dragging so it is not moved by accident.
widget.graphs_desc: Small history graphs for CPU, GPU, RAM, network and disk.
widget.autostart_desc: Open the widget automatically at sign-in (no main window, no UAC prompt).
widget.autostart_on: Enabled: the widget will open when you sign in to Windows.
widget.autostart_off: The widget will no longer start with Windows.
widget.autostart_failed: Could not change the startup task (Task Scheduler).
widget.metrics_desc: Pick what to show on the widget. They appear in this order.
widget.tip: Drag the widget to move it (it snaps to screen edges), double-click to open PC Check, right-click for more options.
widget.empty: No metrics selected. Pick some on the Widget page.
widget.collapse_desc: Show only icons and values in a small grid. Click the arrow on the widget to expand / collapse quickly.
issues.click_hint: Click an issue to see its causes and step-by-step fix.
guide.cpu_hot.cause: A hot CPU is usually caused by dust in the fan and heatsink, thermal paste that dried out after 2–3 years, a failing fan or poor airflow. Background apps keeping the CPU busy also raise the temperature.
guide.cpu_hot.steps:
Open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) → Processes → sort by CPU and close anything using CPU unexpectedly.
Check that the CPU/laptop fan spins without odd noises; see fan speeds on the Temperature & Health page.
Shut down, unplug, and clean dust from the fan, vents and heatsink with a soft brush or compressed air.
PC older than 2–3 years: replace the thermal paste (have a technician do it on laptops).
Laptop: raise the back or use a cooling pad. Desktop: make sure case fans blow in the right direction.
Use the Balanced power plan instead of High performance to reduce heat.
guide.gpu_hot.cause: A hot graphics card is usually caused by dust in the fans and heatsink, a poorly ventilated case, aged thermal paste/pads, or games running at uncapped FPS.
guide.gpu_hot.steps:
Cap the FPS in games or enable V-Sync/G-Sync so the GPU does not run flat out needlessly.
Shut down, unplug, and clean the card's fans and heatsink.
Desktop: arrange case fans so air comes in at the front and leaves at the back/top.
Update the graphics driver to the latest version.
Still hot: use MSI Afterburner / AMD Adrenalin to adjust the fan curve or apply a light undervolt.
guide.cpu_sensor.cause: Windows does not let any software read the CPU's internal temperature sensor without a kernel driver – HWiNFO, Core Temp and AIDA64 all ship their own. Without one, PC Check uses Windows' ACPI thermal zones, which are only an estimate.
guide.cpu_sensor.steps:
Click "Enable accurate CPU temperature".
PC Check downloads the official PawnIO driver (open source, digitally signed) from GitHub and verifies its signature before running it.
The driver installs silently – no need to restart PC Check.
The accurate CPU temperature then appears on the Temperature & Health page and on the widget.
To remove it later: Settings → Apps → Installed apps → PawnIO → Uninstall.
guide.disk_failing.cause: The drive reports bad health through S.M.A.R.T: bad sectors, growing read/write errors or failing components. It may stop working at any moment.
guide.disk_failing.steps:
Back up important data NOW (Documents, Desktop, photos, chat data...) to another drive, a USB stick or Google Drive/OneDrive.
Avoid writing more to this drive; don't defragment it or run "bad sector repair" tools.
Buy a new drive (preferably an SSD) and copy or clone your data with Macrium Reflect, Clonezilla or the SSD vendor's tool.
If it is the system drive: clone to the new drive or reinstall Windows on it.
Desktop: check the SATA and power cables – a loose cable can also trigger errors.
guide.ssd_wear.cause: Every SSD has a limit on total data written (TBW). When most of its life is used, it may slow down or fail.
guide.ssd_wear.steps:
Back up important data regularly.
Check the remaining life every few months on the Temperature & Health page.
Reduce needless writes: move torrent downloads and screen recordings to another drive.
Plan to replace the SSD when less than 10% life remains.
guide.disk_errors.cause: Windows recorded read/write errors or bad sectors – the drive may be starting to fail, a cable/slot may be loose, or power was lost during a write.
guide.disk_errors.steps:
Back up important data first.
Run "Check disk (CHKDSK)" to scan the file system.
Check the drive's S.M.A.R.T health on the Temperature & Health page.
Desktop: reseat or replace the SATA cable and try another SATA port on the motherboard.
If errors keep increasing: replace the drive.
guide.disk_hot.cause: A hot drive is usually caused by poor airflow, an NVMe SSD without a heatsink, or constant reading/writing.
guide.disk_hot.steps:
Check the case fans and the airflow around the drive.
NVMe SSD: fit a heatsink; many motherboards include an M.2 cover.
HDD: don't stack drives tightly, leave space between them.
Keep the PC away from heat sources and closed cabinets.
guide.low_space.cause: A nearly full drive stops Windows from updating, slows the PC and can cause errors when writing temporary files.
guide.low_space.steps:
Go to Cleanup → Junk files, select items and click "Clean up".
Uninstall unused software and games on the Software tab.
Open Settings → System → Storage → turn on Storage Sense so Windows cleans up regularly.
Move photos, videos and the Downloads folder to another drive or cloud storage.
If Windows.old exists: remove it with Disk Cleanup → Clean up system files.
guide.battery.cause: Lithium batteries wear with charge cycles and heat, so real capacity drops below the design capacity.
guide.battery.steps:
Run "Battery report" for a detailed capacity history.
Avoid draining to 0% and avoid sitting at 100% on the charger for long periods.
Enable an 80% charge limit if your vendor's app offers it (Lenovo Vantage, MyASUS, Dell Power Manager...).
Keep the laptop cool while charging; don't use it on blankets or pillows.
Wear above 40% or a swollen battery: replace it with a genuine part.
guide.ram_full.cause: More apps/browser tabs are running than the RAM can hold, or an app is leaking memory.
guide.ram_full.steps:
Open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) → sort by Memory and close heavy apps.
Close extra browser tabs and disable unneeded extensions.
Disable startup programs on Cleanup → Startup programs.
Make sure the page file is enabled and system managed.
If it fills up often: add more RAM (see the Compatibility page for free slots).
guide.gpu_error.cause: Graphics card errors are usually caused by a broken/conflicting driver, a loosely seated card or missing auxiliary power.
guide.gpu_error.steps:
Download the latest driver from NVIDIA / AMD / Intel ("Official driver page" button).
Open Device Manager → Display adapters → right-click the card → Uninstall device, then reinstall the driver.
Desktop: shut down, reseat the card in its PCIe slot and the 6/8-pin power cables.
Laptop with two GPUs: update the integrated Intel/AMD driver too.
Still failing: test the card in another PC to rule out a hardware fault.
guide.driver_missing.cause: Windows has no suitable driver, so the device does not work or lacks features.
guide.driver_missing.steps:
Click "Drivers via Windows Update" → Optional updates → Driver updates, select the related driver and install it.
Or download it from your PC/motherboard vendor's support page (search by model).
Not sure what the device is: click "Search driver online" – it searches by the hardware ID (VEN/DEV) shown above.
After installing: click "Scan for hardware changes" or restart.
guide.driver_error.cause: The device has a driver but cannot start – the driver is broken or incompatible, or the hardware has a problem.
guide.driver_error.steps:
Open Device Manager, right-click the device → Uninstall device (tick delete driver if offered).
Click "Scan for hardware changes" so Windows detects it again.
Install the latest driver from the vendor or Windows Update.
USB devices: try another USB port and cable.
Still failing (especially code 43): the hardware may be faulty.
guide.driver_display.cause: Windows is using the basic display driver because no graphics driver is installed – common after reinstalling Windows.
guide.driver_display.steps:
Click "Official driver page" to download the NVIDIA / AMD / Intel driver for your card.
Or open Windows Update → Advanced options → Optional updates and install the display driver.
Laptop: prefer the driver from the laptop vendor's support page.
Restart, then set resolution and refresh rate in Display settings.
guide.driver_audio.cause: The generic Microsoft audio driver is in use – sound works but mic, jack detection or audio effects may be missing.
guide.driver_audio.steps:
Download the audio driver (usually Realtek) from your PC/motherboard vendor's support page.
Install it and restart.
Check speakers and mic in Settings → System → Sound.
guide.driver_unsigned.cause: Unsigned drivers may be modified, outdated or from unknown sources – they can cause errors, blue screens or security risks.
guide.driver_unsigned.steps:
Note the device names listed.
Download signed official drivers from the vendor or Windows Update.
In Device Manager: right-click the device → Update driver → choose the new driver.
Avoid tools that disable driver signature enforcement unless truly needed.
guide.driver_outdated.cause: Old drivers may lack bug fixes, performance improvements and compatibility with newer Windows.
guide.driver_outdated.steps:
Prioritize graphics, network, audio and chipset drivers.
Download from the vendor (driver page button) or Windows Update → Optional updates.
Avoid advertised "automatic driver updater" tools – they often install the wrong driver.
Create a restore point before updating so you can roll back.
guide.driver_disabled.cause: The device is disabled in Device Manager (by the user, software or policy).
guide.driver_disabled.steps:
Open Device Manager.
Find the device with a down-arrow icon, right-click → Enable device.
If you disabled it on purpose (e.g. a webcam), you can ignore this.
guide.bsod.cause: A blue screen happens when Windows hits an error it cannot recover from – usually a faulty driver, bad RAM, disk errors, overheating or unstable overclocking.
guide.bsod.steps:
Check the stop code in the details and the likely cause above.
Update Windows and drivers (especially graphics, network, chipset).
Run "Repair system files" (DISM + SFC).
Run "Test RAM"; if it finds errors, test one stick at a time.
Check temperatures and drive health; remove any CPU/RAM/GPU overclock.
Started after installing new software/drivers: remove it or use System Restore.
guide.power_loss.cause: The PC turned off without a proper shutdown: power loss, a weak/failing power supply, overheating, a hard freeze needing the power button, or a worn laptop battery.
guide.power_loss.steps:
Think about when it happens: during games/heavy load → suspect the power supply or overheating.
Watch CPU/GPU temperatures under load on the Temperature & Health page or the widget.
Desktop: make sure the PSU is strong enough for the graphics card, try another power cable/outlet, use a UPS if power is unstable.
Laptop: check the charger and battery; try using it while plugged in.
Open "Reliability history" to match the times of the failures.
guide.whea.cause: WHEA errors are reported by the hardware itself (CPU, RAM, PCIe). Even corrected errors are a sign of unstable hardware.
guide.whea.steps:
Remove CPU/RAM overclocks (try disabling XMP) to test.
Run "Test RAM".
Update the BIOS and chipset drivers from the motherboard vendor.
Reseat the graphics card and NVMe SSD; try another PCIe slot.
Check temperatures and the power supply.
guide.storage_reset.cause: The storage controller had to reset an unresponsive drive – usually a loose cable/slot, old SSD firmware or the storage driver.
guide.storage_reset.steps:
Desktop: reseat or replace the SATA cable and try another SATA port.
Update the SSD firmware with the vendor's tool (Samsung Magician, WD Dashboard, Crucial Storage Executive...).
Update chipset / Intel RST / AMD SATA drivers.
Check drive health; if read/write errors also appear, back up now.
guide.ntfs.cause: The NTFS file system structure is damaged, usually after a power loss or forced shutdown.
guide.ntfs.steps:
Run "Check disk (CHKDSK)".
If CHKDSK says repairs are needed: open Command Prompt (Admin), run chkdsk C: /f and restart.
Check the drive's health.
Avoid shutting down by holding the power button.
guide.tdr.cause: The graphics driver hung and Windows had to restart it – a faulty driver, GPU overheating, overclocking or a weak power supply.
guide.tdr.steps:
Install the latest graphics driver (optionally clean-remove the old one with DDU first).
Watch the GPU temperature while gaming.
Remove GPU overclocks or slightly lower clocks with MSI Afterburner.
Desktop: connect all auxiliary power cables and make sure the PSU is strong enough.
guide.app_crash.cause: Internal app bugs, software conflicts, missing runtime libraries or corrupted system files.
guide.app_crash.steps:
Update the app to the latest version, or uninstall and reinstall it.
Install/repair the latest Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable and .NET.
If many apps crash: run "Repair system files" and "Test RAM".
Open "Reliability history" to see when the crashes started.
guide.not_admin.cause: PC Check is running without administrator rights, so some data is missing.
guide.not_admin.steps:
Close PC Check.
Right-click PcCheck.exe → Run as administrator.
guide.windows_eos.cause: This Windows version no longer receives Microsoft security patches – the PC is exposed to malware and vulnerabilities.
guide.windows_eos.steps:
Windows 10: see the Compatibility page to check whether the PC can run Windows 11.
If eligible: Settings → Windows Update → upgrade to Windows 11 (free).
Older Windows 11 version: Settings → Windows Update → install the latest feature update.
Not eligible: consider upgrading the hardware; businesses can buy ESU.
guide.pending_reboot.cause: Updates or system changes only finish after a restart.
guide.pending_reboot.steps:
Save your work.
Click "Restart PC" (or Start → Power → Restart).
guide.uptime.cause: Running for many days accumulates memory clutter, stuck processes and unapplied updates.
guide.uptime.steps:
Restart regularly, at least once a week.
Use Restart instead of Shut down while Fast Startup is on.
guide.no_av.cause: No antivirus is providing real-time protection.
guide.no_av.steps:
Open Windows Security → Virus & threat protection.
Turn on Real-time protection.
If you just removed another antivirus: restart so Microsoft Defender turns back on.
Run a Quick scan.
guide.av_outdated.cause: Virus definitions are out of date, so new malware may go undetected.
guide.av_outdated.steps:
Open Windows Security → Virus & threat protection → Protection updates → Check for updates.
Check the network connection and Windows Update.
guide.firewall.cause: The firewall is off, so the PC is exposed to unauthorized network access, especially on public Wi-Fi.
guide.firewall.steps:
Open Windows Security → Firewall & network protection.
Turn the firewall on for Domain, Private and Public networks.
If an app needs a port: add an allow rule instead of turning the firewall off.
guide.uac.cause: User Account Control is off, so software can run with admin rights without asking.
guide.uac.steps:
Click "UAC settings".
Move the slider to the default level (second from the top) and click OK.
Restart the PC.
guide.activation.cause: Windows does not have a valid license.
guide.activation.steps:
Open Settings → System → Activation.
Enter a product key or sign in with a Microsoft account that holds a digital license.
Just replaced the motherboard: use Troubleshoot on the Activation page.
guide.updates.cause: Windows has not been updated for a long time, so security patches and fixes are missing.
guide.updates.steps:
Open Windows Update → Check for updates and install everything.
If Windows Update fails or is stuck: run "Fix Windows Update".
Keep at least 20 GB free on drive C.
guide.pagefile.cause: The page file is disabled, so apps can close suddenly when RAM runs out.
guide.pagefile.steps:
Click "Performance options" → Advanced tab → Virtual memory → Change.
Select "Automatically manage paging file size for all drives".
Click OK and restart.
guide.windows_old.cause: The previous Windows installation is kept after an upgrade so you can roll back – it takes a lot of space.
guide.windows_old.steps:
Open Settings → System → Storage → Temporary files.
Select "Previous Windows installation(s)" and click Remove files.
Or use Disk Cleanup → Clean up system files.
guide.junk.cause: Temporary files, update caches and browser caches build up over time.
guide.junk.steps:
Go to Cleanup → Junk files.
Review the size of each item and untick anything you want to keep.
Click "Clean up" – files in use are skipped safely.
Close your browsers first to clean more cache.
guide.bloat.cause: Adware, fake "optimizers" and toolbars are often bundled with free software installers.
guide.bloat.steps:
Go to Cleanup → Software → filter "Unwanted".
Click "Uninstall" for each and follow the uninstaller.
Restart and run a virus scan with Windows Security.
Next time you install software, choose Custom and untick bundled offers.
guide.unused.cause: Software you haven't opened for a long time still takes space and may run background services.
guide.unused.steps:
Go to Cleanup → Software → filter "Rarely used".
Review the list and uninstall what you no longer need.
guide.startup.cause: Many apps register themselves to start with Windows, slowing boot and using RAM.
guide.startup.steps:
Go to Cleanup → Startup programs.
Turn off items you don't need right away (chat apps, Teams, Steam, updaters...).
Keep antivirus, audio/touchpad drivers and needed sync tools.
Restart to see the difference.
guide.ram_channel.cause: Only one RAM stick is installed, so memory runs in single channel – half the bandwidth, noticeable in games and with integrated graphics.
guide.ram_channel.steps:
See the RAM type (DDR4/DDR5), speed and size on the Hardware page.
Buy one more stick with the same size and speed (ideally same brand and part number).
Install it in the slots recommended by the motherboard manual (usually A2 and B2).
Rescan to confirm dual channel.
guide.ram_matched.cause: The RAM sticks differ in size/speed – memory runs at the slowest stick's speed and may lose dual channel or be unstable.
guide.ram_matched.steps:
See each stick's details on the Hardware page.
If the PC freezes or blue-screens: test one stick at a time to find a faulty one.
Ideally use a matched kit of identical sticks.
guide.ram_xmp.cause: RAM runs at its default (JEDEC) speed, below the advertised speed, because XMP/EXPO is not enabled in the BIOS.
guide.ram_xmp.steps:
Restart and press Del or F2 to enter the BIOS.
Find XMP (Intel) or EXPO/DOCP (AMD) and select Profile 1.
Save and exit (usually F10).
If the PC won't boot: the BIOS recovers automatically, or choose one speed step lower.
guide.ram_capacity.cause: The amount of RAM is low for Windows 11 and today's browsers.
guide.ram_capacity.steps:
See free slots and maximum capacity on the Compatibility page.
Upgrade to at least 8 GB, 16 GB recommended.
Pick the right type: DDR4/DDR5, DIMM for desktops, SO-DIMM for laptops.
guide.system_hdd.cause: Windows runs on a mechanical hard disk (HDD), so booting and opening apps is slow.
guide.system_hdd.steps:
Buy an SSD (2.5" SATA, or NVMe if the motherboard has an M.2 slot).
Clone the old drive to the SSD with Macrium Reflect / the SSD vendor's tool, or install Windows fresh.
Select the SSD as the boot drive in the BIOS.
Keep the old HDD for data storage.
guide.system_usb.cause: Windows is running from an external USB drive – slow and error-prone if the cable is loose.
guide.system_usb.steps:
Install Windows on an internal drive (preferably an SSD) if possible.
If USB is required: use a USB 3.x port and a solid cable.
guide.os_32bit.cause: 32-bit Windows can only use about 3.5 GB of RAM and many new apps won't run.
guide.os_32bit.steps:
Back up your data.
Download 64-bit Windows from Microsoft (Media Creation Tool).
Clean-install 64-bit Windows (in-place upgrade from 32-bit is not possible).
guide.multi_av.cause: Several real-time antivirus products conflict, slow the PC and cause errors.
guide.multi_av.steps:
Keep only one (the built-in Microsoft Defender is enough for most users).
Uninstall the others on Cleanup → Software (or with the vendor's removal tool).
Restart the PC.
guide.refresh_rate.cause: The display supports a high refresh rate but Windows uses a lower one (usually 60 Hz).
guide.refresh_rate.steps:
Click "Display settings" → Advanced display.
Under "Choose a refresh rate", pick the highest value.
No high option: use a DisplayPort or HDMI 2.0+ cable plugged into the discrete GPU.
Update the graphics driver.
guide.resolution.cause: The resolution is lower than the display's native resolution, so the image and text look blurry.
guide.resolution.steps:
Open Settings → System → Display.
Under Display resolution, choose the (Recommended) option.
Text too small: raise Scale to 125% or 150%.
guide.win11.cause: Summary of the Windows 11 requirements: CPU, TPM 2.0, UEFI, Secure Boot, RAM and storage.
guide.win11.steps:
Review each "Fail" item on the Compatibility page.
TPM and Secure Boot usually just need enabling in the BIOS.
UEFI: convert the disk to GPT with mbr2gpt, then enable UEFI (back up first).
When eligible: Settings → Windows Update to upgrade.
guide.bios_age.cause: A BIOS/UEFI that has not been updated for years may lack security patches, support for newer CPUs/RAM and stability or compatibility fixes.
guide.bios_age.steps:
Find the motherboard / laptop model on the Hardware page.
Open the manufacturer's support page (ASUS, MSI, Gigabyte, Dell, HP, Lenovo...) for that exact model, BIOS section.
Read the release notes: only update when the new version fixes security, stability or adds hardware support you need.
Plug in the charger (laptop) or make sure power is stable; never turn off the PC during the update.
Use the official tool (MyASUS, Dell Update, Lenovo Vantage, M-Flash, Q-Flash...) to update.
Afterwards, open the BIOS and re-check XMP/EXPO, Secure Boot and boot order.
guide.virtualization.cause: CPU virtualization (Intel VT-x / AMD-V, SVM) is disabled in the BIOS, so virtual machines, WSL2, Windows Sandbox and Android emulators cannot run.
guide.virtualization.steps:
Restart the PC and press the BIOS key (usually Del, F2, F10 or Esc).
Find Advanced / CPU Configuration (or Security on laptops).
Enable Intel Virtualization Technology (VT-x) or SVM Mode (AMD).
Save and exit (usually F10).
In Windows, open Task Manager → Performance → CPU and check Virtualization: Enabled.
guide.ram_upgrade.cause: This PC can take more RAM (free slots or below the board's maximum capacity). More RAM keeps many apps and browser tabs running smoothly.
guide.ram_upgrade.steps:
Check the RAM type (DDR4/DDR5), speed and free slots on the Hardware page.
Buy a stick of the same type and speed, ideally the same size as the existing one to run in dual channel.
Shut down, unplug, and touch a metal part of the case to discharge static before installing.
Install the RAM in the slots recommended by the motherboard manual (usually A2 + B2 for two sticks).
Power on, confirm the capacity on the Hardware page and enable XMP/EXPO in the BIOS if needed.
